[Runbook: Kubernetes rollouts that stall and pods that crash loop > Diagnosis: crash loop or image pull]
1. Call `get_k8s_like_events` for the service. `CrashLoopBackOff` means the code starts and
   exits; `BackOff` after an `OOMKilled` termination means memory (see the readiness and
   memory runbook); `ImagePullBackOff` means the image itself.
2. For a crash loop, read `get_service_logs`: the last lines before each exit name the
   error. An exception tagged with a release, such as `[build <release>]` or
   `(version=<release>)`, points at the code of that release.
3. For an image-pull back-off the logs are empty. Compare the newest revision with the one
   before it in `get_recent_deployments`.
4. Compare times with `get_recent_deployments` and the `error_rate` metric. A crash loop
   that begins within minutes of the service's own release makes that release a suspect. A
   crash loop on a service that was not released points elsewhere: memory, configuration, or
   a dependency it needs at start-up.

[Runbook: memory pressure and crash loops > Overview]
Memory pressure means a container is using nearly all of its memory limit. When it
crosses the limit it is killed and restarted, and if the leak continues the pod ends up
in a crash loop.
</untrusted_data>
<untrusted_data id="runbook-memory-pressure#symptoms-1" kind="doc" flags="" source="doc:fixtures/knowledge/runbook-memory-pressure.md#Symptoms">
[Runbook: memory pressure and crash loops > Symptoms]
- `OOMKilled` events: a container exceeded its memory limit and was killed.
- `BackOff` events and a `CrashLoopBackOff` status while the pod keeps restarting.
- Readiness probe failures, so fewer replicas are ready than desired.
- The memory metric climbs toward the limit; logs show heap warnings and
  `OutOfMemoryError` lines.
- The error rate rises because the remaining replicas take all the traffic.
</untrusted_data>
